newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Markets cheered by on-target S.Africa budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Markets cheered by on-target S.Africa budget.

text.p: Finance Minister Trevor Manuel gave bullish South African markets a fresh lease of life on Thursday, announcing that the government would meet its budget deficit target in the year to end-March.

Presenting his Appropriations Adjustment Bill in parliament, Manuel said the government had revised its 1996/97 expenditure upwards by 2.4 billion rand ($615 million) to 176.1 billion rand but was still on target to achieve a deficit of 5.1 percent of gross domestic product.
The higher expenditure would be offset by a 2.5 billion rand increase in revenues to 147.4 billion rand from the 144.9 billion estimated initially, he said.
"The budget deficit is expected to amount to 28.7 billion rand, or 5.1 percent of GDP, as planned," Manuel told MPs.
"The achievement of our deficit target represents an important step in establishing the sound fiscal and financial framework within which our growth, employment and redistribution goals can be met."
Manuel earlier told reporters the actual outcome for the current fiscal year could be even better than 5.1 percent, depending on final figures.
Government bond prices raced to their best levels since July 3, 1996, well ahead of the budget speech, with particularly heavy buying noted from overseas banks.

Manuel also announced the cancellation of 3.1 billion rand of unspent allocations from previous years. Of the 12 billion rand not spent in 1995/96, only 8.9 billion rand is being recommended for rollover into 1996/97.
A further nine billion rand of spending budgeted for 1996/97 is not expected to be requested by departments or will be surrendered back to the exchequer.
Manuel signalled that the government intended to cut rollovers further in the future, thereby reducing the risk of over-spending by departments in future years.

"It is recognised that an amount of nine billion rand, although significantly reduced from the unspent balance at the end of 1995/96, represents a large potential source of rollovers to the 1997/98 year," he said.
"Requests for rolling over these funds will be scrutinised thoroughly, with a view to bringing the gap between available budgeted amounts and actual spending outlays down to more acceptable limits."
Manuel said the strong revenue collection performance reflected an improvement in tax collection by the South African Revenue Services and changes in sources of income.
